title: Two bishops: the wall and the corner
summary: Bishops side by side shut the door; the king pushes all the way to a corner.
part.mates.title: The destination: three mating patterns
part.mates.summary: Before the road, the destination: where the black king ends up, and which patterns can be forced.
part.wall.title: The wall
part.wall.summary: Bishops side by side make a wall; the king walks around it and stands in front of it.
part.build.title: Building the wall from scratch
part.build.summary: With the pieces at home, the king comes out first and the bishops reach the centre, always protected.
part.edge.title: Down to the corner
part.edge.summary: The bishops step down one at a time, the king follows, and the black king ends in the corner mate.
part.far.title: The bishops hold from afar
part.far.summary: Two neighbouring diagonals make a wall at any distance, while the king is still on its way.
part.ahead.title: Close the exit before the check
part.ahead.summary: The natural check opens a door; a quiet bishop move closes it first.
part.stalemate.title: Count the squares
part.stalemate.summary: Near the corner, with one square left: check or wait. And the king comes round the outside, without stalemate.
part.finish.title: How a grandmaster finishes
part.finish.summary: The rules of the lesson, Nakamura's ending and the practical challenge.
step.t_mates: Before learning the road, let's look at the destination. The black king is on h8, cornered by your bishops and your king, and has no free square. One move ends the game here. Which one?
step.t_mates.hint1: Count the squares around h8: g8, g7 and h7. Who takes each of them?
step.t_mates.hint2: Most moves that are not a check leave the black king with no move and not in check, and that is a draw. Look for a check that keeps g8 covered.
step.mateCorner: This is the corner mate, and it comes from a real game: Hikaru Nakamura against Ethan Sheehan, in an online tournament, in July 2024. Nakamura finished with 64.Bd4#. The white king on f7 takes g7 and g8, the bishop on e4 takes h7, and the bishop on d4 gives check along the long diagonal. The bishops end side by side, like a wall pushed against the corner. With two bishops any corner will do: one bishop of each colour covers both colours of squares.
step.mateSide: The second pattern is on the square next to the corner. Black king on b8, your king on b6, the light bishop on b7, protected by the king, taking a8 and c8, and the dark bishop giving check from d6. This one can be forced too: the black king that runs from the corner ends up here.
step.mateEdge: There is a third pattern, in the middle of the edge. The light bishop checks from afar, from b5. The dark one, on e7 and protected by the king, takes d8 and f8. Reuben Fine, in his book Basic Chess Endings, showed that this mate exists but cannot be forced: with the black king free on the edge, it always has somewhere to go. It only happens when the black king is already trapped there. That is why the technique takes the black king to the corner.
step.cornerMate: Back to the first position: give the corner mate.
step.cornerMate.hint: The dark bishop enters the long diagonal and gives check; the light one already holds g8.
step.cornerMate.done: 1.Be5#. The dark bishop checks along the long diagonal and the light one holds g8 from afar: it is the corner mate, as in Nakamura's game. Sixteen moves here stalemated the black king, and 1.Bg8 gave the bishop away. Near the corner, every move counts.
step.t_wall: Now the tool that takes the black king to the corner. Your bishops stand side by side in the centre, on d5 and e5, and the black king is on d7. Which squares do the bishops take from it, and who will push it from here?
step.t_wall.hint1: Follow the four diagonals of the bishops and mark the squares they take. Notice which side the black king is left on.
step.t_wall.hint2: The black king is trapped. Who can push it without crossing the bishops' diagonals?
step.wall: You already gave this mate at school. Now let's understand why it works. One bishop moves on the light squares, the other on the dark ones, and their diagonals cross like an X. The black king on d7 is trapped in a small strip: c8, d8, e8, f8, d7 and e7. It cannot cross the diagonals. That is the wall, and it stands without the white king's help. The king comes afterwards, to push.
step.d_join: The white king does not go through the wall. It walks around the side. Watch, I play both sides.
step.d_join.m1: 1.Kf5 climbs the f-file, next to the bishop on e5, without crossing any diagonal. It is the fastest move.
step.d_join.m2: 1...Kc8. The black king runs away from the white king, towards a8.
step.d_join.m3: 2.Ke6 puts the king in front of the bishops, facing the black king. Now it takes d7, e7 and f7.
step.d_join.m4: 2...Kd8 is the only move. The black king is on the edge and will not get back to the centre.
step.joinMove: Another wall, with the bishops on c5 and d5, and the black king on f6, on the upper side. Bring your king in front of it, round the outside.
step.joinMove.hint: The king climbs the f-file, facing the black king, without crossing the diagonals.
step.joinMove.done: 1.Kf4! Your king closes the front of the wall. The black king is left with f6, g6, g7 and the h-file, and can only go to g6 or g7.
step.t_build: So far the wall was already built. In a game you have to build it. White's pieces are at home and the black king is in the centre, on d4. Where do the bishops want to go, and who leaves home first?
step.t_build.hint1: Remember the wall: bishops side by side, in the centre.
step.t_build.hint2: On the way, the bishops need the king nearby, or the black king attacks them.
step.build: This is the position Yasser Seirawan uses in his book Winning Chess Endings to teach this mate. The king leaves home first. The bishops go to the centre without hurry, each one to a square the king protects, and each of their moves pushes the black king back a little. The black king will try to stay in the middle.
step.d_build: These are Seirawan's moves. I play both sides.
step.d_build.m1: 1.Ke2. The king leaves home first, heading for the centre, to protect the bishops that come next.
step.d_build.m2: 1...Ke4. The black king tries to stay in the centre.
step.d_build.m3: 2.Be3 takes d4 and f4 and pushes the black king back. The bishop is protected by the king.
step.d_build.m4: 2...Ke5. The black king has to step back to the fifth rank: the fourth has no free square left for it.
step.d_build.m5: 3.Kd3. The king follows, protects the bishop and takes e4.
step.d_build.m6: 3...Kd5. The black king looks for another central square.
step.d_build.m7: 4.Bd4 puts the dark bishop in the centre, protected by the king: the black king stands next to it but cannot take it.
step.d_build.m9: 5.Ke4. The king goes in front of the bishop and takes d5, e5 and f5.
step.d_build.m10: 5...Kd6. The black king tries another way to stay near the middle.
step.d_build.m11: 6.Bc4. The light bishop, which was far away, arrives next to the dark one. The bishops stand side by side on c4 and d4, the king is active, and the wall is built: the black king is trapped in the upper part, on the queenside.
step.buildMove: Now you build. The white king is already in the centre, on e4, but the bishops are still on the first rank, and the black king is on c4. Bring a bishop to the centre without giving the black king a chance to attack it.
step.buildMove.hint: A bishop goes to a central square next to your king, which protects it, and cuts squares from the black king.
step.buildMove.done: 1.Bd4! The bishop reaches the centre protected by the king, takes c3 and c5, and the black king has to retreat to b4 or b5, away from the middle. Now the light bishop comes next to it, and the wall is ready.
step.t_edge: We are back at the wall from part 2, after 2.Ke6 Kd8, and the black king is on the edge. Which corner do you want to take it to, and which square must you close first so it doesn't run to the other side?
step.t_edge.hint1: The black king wants to go to a8 or to h8. Choose a corner and close the way to the other.
step.t_edge.hint2: A bishop, from afar, can take c8 without leaving the long diagonal.
step.edgeTalk: At the wall, after 2.Ke6 Kd8, we choose the h8 corner. First the light bishop closes c8, so the black king cannot go towards a8. Then the bishops step down one at a time, and the white king follows along the sixth rank. No bishop comes close to the black king: they work from afar.
step.d_edge: The wall steps down, after 2.Ke6 Kd8, one bishop at a time. I play both sides.
step.d_edge.m1: 3.Bb7 takes c8. The way to a8 is closed.
step.d_edge.m2: 3...Ke8 is the only move: c8 belongs to the bishop on b7, c7 to the bishop on e5, and d7 and e7 to the white king.
step.d_edge.m3: 4.Bc7 takes d8 and b8. The black king only has f8: it is being pushed towards h8.
step.d_edge.m5: 5.Kf6. The king follows without hurry, from the side, and takes e7, f7 and g7. It is the fastest move.
step.d_edge.m6: 5...Ke8. The black king tries to get back to the middle.
step.d_edge.m8: 6...Kf8 is the only move: d8 belongs to the bishop on c7, d7 is on the line of the check, and e7 and f7 belong to the white king.
step.d_edge.m9: 7.Bd7. From d7 the bishop takes e8 for good, without giving check.
step.d_edge.m10: 7...Kg8. What is left is f8, g8, h8 and the h-file, and the white king's next move closes the h-file.
step.mate: Another box in the same corner: the black king on g8, your king on f6, the bishops on b8 and e4. Take the black king to h8 and give the corner mate, without stalemate.
step.mate.hint: Before any check, close f8 with a quiet move. Then your king comes in front of the black king, leaving g8 free.
step.mate.done: 1.Bd6! Kh8 2.Kg6! Kg8 3.Bd5+ Kh8 4.Be5#. The quiet move closed f8, and 2.Kf7?? would stalemate. The bishops end side by side on d5 and e5, as in Nakamura's game.
step.t_far: So far your king was always close. What if it is far away? Your king is on c1, the bishops on a6 and h6, and the black king on g4, away from the edge. Find the bishop move that shuts the black king in a corner without the king's help.
step.t_far.hint1: The bishop on h6 already cuts a whole diagonal, from h6 down to c1. Where does the black king get across it?
step.t_far.hint2: Look for a square for the light bishop where its diagonal runs right next to the dark bishop's diagonal.
step.far: The dark bishop, from h6, cuts the whole diagonal down to c1: g5, f4, e3 and d2. To get to the other side, the black king must step on the light squares of the neighbouring diagonal, from b1 to h7: e4, f5 or g6. If the light bishop occupies that neighbouring diagonal, the two neighbouring diagonals make a slanted wall, like the wall in the centre, only from afar. Remember the wall: what matters is that the diagonals are neighbours, not that the bishops stand together.
step.d_far: The bishops close the box and shrink it on their own. Only then does the king come. I play both sides.
step.d_far.m1: 1.Bd3! The diagonal from b1 to h7 now runs next to the dark bishop's diagonal. The bishop takes f5, and the black king is left in the h1 corner, with twelve squares.
step.d_far.m2: 1...Kh5. The black king attacks the bishop on h6, which is alone.
step.d_far.m3: 2.Bd2! The bishop leaves the attack along the same diagonal, far from the black king, and also takes e1. A bishop far away is a safe bishop.
step.d_far.m4: 2...Kh4. The black king looks for an exit that does not exist.
step.d_far.m5: 3.Be2. The light bishop steps down to the next diagonal and takes f3, g4 and h5. The box shrinks, without a check.
step.d_far.m6: 3...Kh3. Now g4 and h5 belong to the bishop on e2, and g5 to the bishop on d2: the black king only has g3 and h3.
step.d_far.m7: 4.Be3. The dark bishop takes f2 and g1. What is left is g2, g3 and the squares h1 to h4.
step.d_far.m8: 4...Kh4. The black king walks inside the box.
step.d_far.m9: 5.Kd2. Only now does the white king come. The bishops hold everything on their own, and it can walk without hurry.
step.d_far.m10: 5...Kh3. The black king is still trapped, and the white king will arrive via e1 and f1.
step.farMove: On the other side of the board: your king is on a3, the black king on c7, and the bishops on e8 and e1. With one bishop move, shut the black king in the a8 corner.
step.farMove.hint: The bishop on e8 already cuts d7, c6 and b5. The dark one has to cut the dark squares below the black king, from afar.
step.farMove.done: 1.Bb4! From the other side, the dark bishop cuts d6, e7 and f8; the light one, from e8, cuts d7, c6 and b5. The black king is left in the a8 corner, with nine squares, and your king is still on a3.
step.t_ahead: The bishops already know how to hold from afar. Now, the right moment for the check. The black king is on the edge, on e8. Your king is on h6, and the bishops on h4 and b1. The check 1.Bg6+ looks natural. Why is it bad, and what should you do first?
step.t_ahead.hint1: After 1.Bg6+, where does the black king go, and where does it go after that?
step.t_ahead.hint2: Right now the black king has d7, f7 and f8. Which of those squares leads back to the centre?
step.t_ahead.hint3: A quiet move of the light bishop can take d7 without giving check and without freeing any square.
step.ahead: After 1.Bg6+ the black king goes to d7 and back to the centre. Everything starts over, and the mate takes eleven moves longer. The right way is to close the exit first and only then give check. The light bishop, from f5, takes d7 without giving check, and the black king is trapped on the kingside.
step.d_check: First, the mistake. I play both sides.
step.d_check.m1: 1.Bg6+? The check pushes the black king, but leaves d7 open.
step.d_check.m2: 1...Kd7. The black king has left the edge and goes back to the centre. The wall has to be built again.
step.d_ahead: Now the right way: the door before the check.
step.d_ahead.m1: 1.Bf5! No check, but it takes d7. The black king is left with e8, f7, f8, g8 and h8.
step.d_ahead.m2: 1...Kf7. The black king stays as far from the corner as it can.
step.d_ahead.m3: 2.Bd7. The bishop takes e8 and e6, again without check. What is left is f7, f8, g8 and h8.
step.d_ahead.m4: 2...Kf8. The black king only had f8 and g8, and neither takes it back to the centre.
step.d_ahead.m5: 3.Kg6. The king arrives and takes f7, g7 and h7.
step.d_ahead.m6: 3...Kg8. It is the f8, g8, h8 box from part 4, and the mate comes in a few moves.
step.aheadMove: The same idea, on the bottom edge and with the other bishop. The black king is on e1 and right now has d2 and f1. The check 1.Bb4+ looks natural, but it frees a square. Close the exit first, then bring the king.
step.aheadMove.hint: The dark bishop can take d2 and keep taking f2, without giving check.
step.aheadMove.done: 1.Be3! Kf1 2.Kg3. The bishop closed d2 and f2, and the black king was left with only e1 and f1. With 1.Bb4+ the bishop left the f2 diagonal, and the black king got out that way. First the door, then the check.
step.t_stalemate: The technique is in place. What is left is the most common way to throw it away. Jeremy Silman shows this position. The black king is in the corner, trapped by the bishops and our king. Before you move: which natural move here would throw the win away?
step.t_stalemate.hint1: Count the black king's squares after each of your moves. If none is left and there is no check, it's a draw.
step.t_stalemate.hint2: Look at the king moves: which one looks natural and takes the last square?
step.stalemate: Stalemate is the most common way to throw this ending away. The black king is on a8 and only has a7. 1.Kb6?? looks natural, because the white king comes closer. But the king on b6 takes a7, and the black king has no move at all, without being in check. Stalemate, a draw. Rule: near the corner, before every move, count the black king's squares. If only one is left, your next move is either a check or leaves that square free. The rule applies to the king too: it comes close round the outside, without taking the last square.
step.d_approach: In Seirawan's line, after 12.Bc6 Kc8, the black king only has d8. 13.Ke7?? would stalemate, because it takes d8. The white king has to come round the outside. I play both sides.
step.d_approach.m1: 13.Kd5! The king steps back to go round the outside, and d8 stays free. It is the fastest move.
step.d_approach.m2: 13...Kd8. The black king uses the square we left.
step.d_approach.m3: 14.Kc5. The king continues along the c-file, away from the black king's last square.
step.d_approach.m4: 14...Kc8 is the only move: c7 and e7 belong to the bishop on d6, and d7 and e8 to the bishop on c6.
step.d_approach.m5: 15.Kb6. It has arrived on b6, from where it watches a7, b7 and c7, and the black king still has d8. No stalemate.
step.d_approach.m6: 15...Kd8. Now the bishops do the rest, pushing the black king to the a8 corner.
step.waiting: Back to Silman's position. You already know that 1.Kb6?? stalemates. Count the black king's squares and play a move that wins.
step.waiting.hint: The black king only has a7. Make a move that does not take that square and changes nothing: a bishop can wait.
step.waiting.done: 1.Bd3! Ka7. A move that does nothing was the most important one: with one square left, wait. Other waiting moves win too, such as 1.Bd6 or 1.Be2; 1.Kb6?? stalemates and 1.Bb8?? gives the bishop away.
step.rules: Four rules to take to your games. First: bishops side by side, in the centre, make a wall the black king cannot cross, and your king goes in front of it. Second: the bishops work from afar and step down one at a time, until the black king is in a box next to a corner, any corner. Third: before giving check, close the square the black king would run to. Fourth: near the corner, count its squares; with only one, check or wait, and bring the king round the outside.
step.naka: Now watch a grandmaster using these rules. Hikaru Nakamura against Ethan Sheehan, in an online tournament, in July 2024. Black had only one pawn, and Nakamura captured it with 57.Bxh2: he was left with king and two bishops against king. The black king is on h6, already on the edge.
step.d_naka: These are the game's moves. I play both sides.
step.d_naka.m1: 58.Be5. The bishop goes back to the centre and takes g7. 58.Kf6 was a little faster, but the plan is the same.
step.d_naka.m2: 58...Kh7. The black king stays near the corner.
step.d_naka.m3: 59.Kf6. The king follows from the side and takes g7, g6 and g5. It is the fastest move.
step.d_naka.m4: 59...Kh6. The black king goes back to h6 to stay away from the corner; g6 and g7 belong to the white king.
step.d_naka.m5: 60.Bf4+. The check pushes the king back to h7. The h5 square is closed by the bishop on f3.
step.d_naka.m6: 60...Kh7. The black king only has g8 and h8. Four moves later, Nakamura gave the corner mate from part 1, with 64.Bd4#.
step.playWall: The whole wall position, in the practical challenge. Your opponent will not follow the lesson's path: it looks for the most stubborn defence. Keep the wall, bring the king and take the black king to any corner.
step.playCenter: Now from the start, as in part 3, in Seirawan's position. Build the wall, bring the king, take the black king to the corner and count the squares before each move.
ex.e04: White to play and win. The black king is on h8 and only has h7. There is a natural move that draws. Find one that wins.
ex.e04.hint: Taking h7 with the light bishop leaves the black king with no move and no check. Before that, give a check or wait with the dark bishop.
ex.e04.solution: 1.Bg7+ forces 1...Kh7, and then 2.Bd3 is mate: the bishop on g7, protected by your king, takes h6 and h8. A waiting move with the dark bishop, or 1.Kg6, also wins. What you cannot play is 1.Bd3 right now: stalemate.
ex.e12: White to play and mate quickly. The black king is on d1, far from the corner. Careful: one bishop move gives stalemate.
ex.e12.hint: The black king has only one free square. A check with the light bishop, protected by your king, sends him there; then the dark bishop comes along the other diagonal.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Be2+ forces 1...Ke1, and 2.Bg3 is mate: the bishop on g3 checks along the e1–h4 diagonal, and the bishop on e2, protected by the king on d3, covers d1 and f1. This is the third mating picture with two bishops, in the middle of the edge. Reuben Fine already showed that it exists but cannot be forced in a game: here it happens because the black king was already trapped. 1.Bd2 on the first move was stalemate.
ex.e13: White to play. The black king on d1 is trapped in the bottom corner, but there is an open door to the center. Find the only move that closes it.
ex.e13.hint: The dark bishop already covers d2 and e1. Where does the black king get out? Follow the light squares and close the exit with the bishop that is far away.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Bc4! From far away the light bishop covers d3 and e2, and the black king is left with c1, c2 and b1: the dark bishop on c3 takes care of d2, e1, b2 and a1. Any other move lets the black king escape through e2 and costs nine more moves (1.Bd2 and 1.Be1 even give away the dark bishop). The bishops do not need to be close to the king to trap it.
ex.e14: White to play and win. The black king on a8 only has a7. Two moves give stalemate and a natural check wastes time. Find the fast way.
ex.e14.hint: Before checking, take away a6, the square the black king will want later. Do it without touching a7.
ex.e14.solution: 1.Bb5! covers a6 and leaves a7 free. 1...Ka7, 2.Bc5+ Ka8 (a6 is already closed) and 3.Bc6 is mate. 1.Bb8 or 1.Bc5 now gave stalemate; 1.Bc6+ right away let the king out through a7 and a6 and cost four more moves.
ex.e15: White to play and win. The black king on b1 only has a2. Almost every move works slowly, one gives stalemate and only one is fast. Find it and take the idea all the way to mate.
ex.e15.hint: The black king is going to climb the a-file. Use the light bishop to cover a square further up the a-file in advance, without taking a2 now.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Bb5! Ka2, 2.Kc2 Ka3, 3.Bc5+ Ka2, 4.Bc4+ Ka1, 5.Bd4 mate. The bishop on b5 covers a4 before the king gets there; your king closes the b-file; the two checks push the king back into the corner. 1.Bc4 on the first move was stalemate, and the check 1.Bd3+ is three moves slower.
ex.e16: White to play and win. The black king is on h1. Bring your king and mate without stalemate: two natural king moves draw.
ex.e16.hint: Count the black king's squares before every king move. Come closer from the outside, through f3 and g3, and use the light bishop to close f1.
ex.e16.solution: 1.Kf3! Kg1, 2.Be2 Kh1, 3.Kg3 Kg1, 4.Be3+ Kh1, 5.Bf3 mate. 1.Kf2 or 1.Kf1 at the start gave stalemate, and 3.Kf2 again on the third move too. 2.Be2 covers f1 and leaves the black king only g1 and h1; the rest is the corner picture.
ex.e17: White to play. The black king is in the center, on d4, and the light bishop is out of place. Find the shortest way: two moves of yours, and each one is the only one.
ex.e17.hint: Put the light bishop next to the dark one, on a square that takes d5 and e4. Then the king goes to the side where the wall is open.
ex.e17.solution: 1.Bc6! Kc4, 2.Ke3! With the bishops side by side on c6 and d6, the black king only has the queenside; from e3 your king covers d3 and d4 and closes the last exit. Any other first move costs at least four more moves, and 1.Bc4, 1.Bc5+ or 1.Be5+ give away a bishop. On the second move, 2.Kc2 or 2.Ke2 cost two moves.
key.wall: The two bishops side by side form a wall the black king can't cross. That's the heart of the method.
key.mateCorner: Mate in the corner: the bishops, side by side, give check and take the last squares, and the white king covers the rest.
key.mateSide: Mate on the square next to the corner: one bishop, protected by the king, sits next to the black king, and the other checks from afar.
key.stalemate: The stalemate trap: with the black king in the corner, one careless step by the white king takes its last square without giving check. Draw.
key.seirawan: White's pieces on their home squares and the black king in the centre: the bishops build the wall, and the king pushes Black to the edge and then into the corner.
history: With two bishops and the king you can mate the lone king, but only by driving it into a corner, and the road is a little long. In practice the ending is rare, and authors disagree on whether it's worth studying: James Howell left it out of his book, while Jeremy Silman taught it. Whoever studies it gains something valuable: you learn how two bishops together form a wall the king can't cross, the famous power of the bishop pair. Reuben Fine, back in the 1940s, already warned in a classic book that two bishops of the same colour can never mate, not even nine of them. And the usual danger is still here: with the black king cornered, one careless move stalemates it.
practice: Now the real ending. The black king is in the centre and your bishops are still far apart. Bring the bishops together, bring your king, and take the black king to a corner without stalemating. Choose the time control and race the clock, or set up your own training.
